planck.classroomUse: Start a discussion about the limits of knowledge: what does it mean when no experiment can reach a scale? Students separate what has been measured from what is speculation using the evidence badges.

proton.classroomUse: Show that protons and neutrons are not the end of the story. Ask: what evidence tells us there is anything inside a proton, if we can never see it?

nucleus.classroomUse: Zoom from the atom to its nucleus and count the particles in carbon-12. Students compare the size of the nucleus with the size of the whole atom.

atom.classroomUse: Use the probability-cloud picture to compare with the planetary (Bohr) model students already know, and discuss why scientists replaced it as evidence improved.

dna.classroomUse: Dive from a cell to the DNA double helix. Students relate the shape of the helix (two strands, paired bases) to how it stores and copies information.

cell.classroomUse: Pair with a microscope lesson. Students name organelles in the scene and estimate how many cells would fit across a pin head.

human.classroomUse: Use as the anchor for the whole tool: every other size is described as a number of powers of ten bigger or smaller than a person. Zoom in to see how organs, tissues and cells nest.

earth.classroomUse: Locate Wollongong on the globe, then link day, night and seasons to the relative positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon. Compare the size of Earth with the Moon using the Compare tray.

sun.classroomUse: Compare the Sun and Earth with the Compare tray ("109 Earths fit across the Sun"). Discuss where the energy in sunlight comes from.

solar-system.classroomUse: Contrast the scale of the Solar System with textbook diagrams, which squash distances. Students compare historical and current models using the nesting notes.

milky-way.classroomUse: Use the time and light layer to show that looking far away means looking back in time. Ask students where in the galaxy the Solar System sits.

universe.classroomUse: Finish the journey at the edge of the observable universe. Link to the Big Bang and the formation of the first elements, and discuss why we can only see a limited part of the universe.

needsTeacherCheck.reason: None of the owner's sequence documents has a dot point about the Planck scale, quantum gravity or the limits of measurement. Left unmapped.

No dot point in the owner's sources is about galaxies. Y10 7.3.4 (learning about stars from the electromagnetic spectrum) is the nearest verified dot point, but it is about stars, so it is not applied automatically.
